electronics.quote: The quantum circuits are programmed with a control infrastructure consisting of five arbitrary waveform generators (AWG) (Spectrum Instrumentation), as illustrated in ED Fig. 1b, synchronized to $<$ 10-ns jitter.

The 2-channel rearrangement AWG is used for real-time rearrangement, the 2 channels of the Rydberg AWG are used for entangling gate pulses and for local SLM detunings, the 4 channels of the Raman AWG are used for IQ (in-phase and quadrature) control of a 6.8 GHz source [67, 35] (the global phase reference for all qubits) and pulse-shaping of the global and local Raman driving, the 2 channels of the Raman AOD AWG are used for displaying tones that create the programmable light grids for local single-qubit control, and the 2 channels of the Moving AOD AWG are used for controlling the positions of all atoms during the circuit.
For this work, we upgrade our microwave source (Rohde and Schwarz, SMW200A)
The entire waveform for all AWGs (except for rearrangement) is uploaded at the start of each experimental run.
For mid-circuit rearrangement, waveforms are calculated on-the-fly using a desktop computer and sent to the Rearrangement AWG operated in first-in first-out (FIFO) mode.
We fill the entire memory of the Spectrum AWG and this is what limits our experiments to 27 layers here (and then we choose an appropriately sized reservoir to have atoms for that many layers).

In the deep circuit experiments in Figure 6, our cycle rate was bottlenecked through the use of desktop computers for all data processing for the mid-circuit image analysis and rearrangement, and so we did not attempt to reduce any times.
cooling and re-sorting takes 13.3-ms ( $\approx$ 7-ms latency for mid-circuit data processing)
Waveforms are uploaded to different segments of the AWG using the SEGMENT[] command, which can then be individually looped or triggered with an external trigger.

decoding.summary: All decoding described in the paper is applied to recorded shots after the experiment (offline): delayed-erasure MLE, a neural-network (ML) decoder, and a hybrid of the two for the surface code; a CNN for the deep circuits. The paper reports no real-time (in-the-loop) decoding; logical feedforward is applied in software (Pauli-frame tracking). The only real-time classical processing in the loop is mid-circuit image analysis + rearrangement on a desktop computer (~7 ms latency) in the deep-circuit experiments.

quotes.quote: We construct the circuit error model using Stim [88] to initially contain information about the Pauli error sources in the circuit, then update it for each shot to reflect the detected atom losses.

quotes.quote: The error probabilities in these channels are then treated as variables which we optimize using the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy [89] in order to minimize the logical error rate on a dataset of approximately 10000 shots (different shots from the final dataset used for evaluating the fidelity).

quotes.quote: We do not detect erasures as soon as they occur, instead we detect them at the final qubit measurement, constituting delayed-erasure information.

Second, we obtain $Z_{1}^{L}Z_{2}^{L}$ directly from the data qubit measurements, using the prior ancilla measurements in decoding.

results.name: below-threshold ratio d=3/d=5
results.quote: We find that $d$ =5 has a 2.14(13)x lower error per round than $d$ =3, indicating below-threshold behavior for this four-round characterization circuit (Fig. 2d).

results.name: LEPR d=5 (hybrid ML+MLE, with loss)
results.quote: This results in a final value for the reported LEPR of 0.62(3)% for $d=5$ and 1.33(4)% for $d=3$ , which corresponds to the ML with loss decoder reported in Fig. 2.

results.name: LEPR definition
results.quote: In Figs. 2d,e, the logical error per round is calculated as $\mathrm{LEPR}=0.5(1-(1-2p_{L})^{1/r})$ where $p_{L}$ is the final logical error after $r=4$ rounds, same as the definition in Ref. [7].

results.name: LEPR ensembled / fine-tuned ML
results.quote: The resulting ensembled ML decoder achieves a logical error per round (LEPR) of 0.78(4)% for $d=5$ and 1.37(3)% for $d=3$ .

results.name: loss + ML improvement
results.quote: In particular, we find that the loss information and machine learning decoding together improve the QEC performance by a factor of 1.73(13)x compared to conventional methods.

results.name: MLE ratio with loss info
results.quote: We find the loss information improves the measured $d=3/d=5$ error ratio from $1.24(5)$ to $1.69(8)$ .
results.section: Methods / Decoding / MLE and error-model tuning

results.name: no-loss shots
results.quote: The error per round is 0.62(3)% for $d=5$ , and reduces toward 0.1% per round on shots with no qubit loss (Fig. 2e), consistent with a $p^{3}$ scaling and roughly half of our errors being loss.

results.name: datasets
results.quote: The $d=5$ dataset contains 9021 shots in the X basis and 5834 in the Z basis. The $d=3$ dataset contains 2523 shots for X and 2534 for Z (on average per quadrant).

results.name: detectors
results.quote: approximately $10^{5}$ detector rounds (14855 shots, 96 detectors per shot across 5 rounds)

results.name: mean detector error (supercheck)
results.quote: using the supercheck metric reveals a 9.04% mean detector error, comparable to the 8.5-8.7% mean detector error in Ref. [7].

results.name: CZ fidelity
results.quote: Although we achieve CZ fidelities of 99.6%, drifts since the last calibration (several days in the context of the surface code benchmarking) often contribute

results.name: local single-qubit gates
results.quote: Local single-qubit gates are approximately 99.9% fidelity, arising from a 0.05% scattering error and residual miscalibrations.

results.name: movement loss (ancillas)
results.quote: We experience a total loss from movement of roughly 1% on the ancilla atoms, arising from transfers and moves between and within the zones.

results.name: readout (spin-to-position)
results.quote: This non-destructive readout has 0.46(4)% bit-flip error and 0.24(2)% loss (Methods).

results.name: leakage that is loss
results.quote: We observe that with several hundred microseconds between gates, effects of Rydberg leakage are not apparent, and during our repeated QEC data we observe that our leakage is at least 80% loss (ED Fig. 5b).
results.section: Methods / Loss detection for improved QEC

results.name: lattice surgery vs transversal
results.quote: We observe a lower logical error for transversal gates, and that the lattice surgery is significantly more sensitive to injected measurement errors.

results.name: lattice surgery protocol
results.quote: In the lattice surgery approach, we carry out a $Z^{1}_{L}Z^{2}_{L}$ joint logical measurement using two rounds of stabilizer measurements [10]. We then measure the $X^{1}_{L}X^{2}_{L}$ and $Z^{1}_{L}Z^{2}_{L}$ parities of the resulting logical Bell state for both methods.

results.name: lattice surgery layout
results.quote: We start with both codes prepared in $\ket{+_{L}}$ and perform two rounds of stabilizer checks on the effective $d\times 2d$ surface code lattice, measuring both the codes’ stabilizer checks and the new seam checks in each round.
results.section: Methods / Decoding / MLE decoder - lattice surgery

results.name: lattice surgery error detection
results.quote: In Fig. 3d, the lattice surgery point uses error detection on the middle three ancillas each having the same value in both rounds of stabilizer measurement, to compensate for having fewer than $d$ rounds of repeated syndrome measurement for this result.

results.name: optimal CNOTs per round
results.quote: observe that approximately three CNOTs per round is optimal at low error rates (Fig. 3d).

results.name: CHSH (error-corrected)
results.quote: measure a CHSH inequality of $1.99(3)\times\sqrt{2}$ , saturating the quantum bound [47].
